newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: El Nino seen as little risk to Colombian coffee.
newsitem.headline: El Nino seen as little risk to Colombian coffee.

text.p: BOGOTA, July 2 Reuter - As meteorologists warn of severe droughts in the face of a new El Nino phenomenon, Colombian coffee experts say there is little risk to the country's key coffee crop.

The cyclical weather pattern, sparked by warming of the Pacific Ocean, could even have a beneficial effect on the harvest depending on when it strikes, researchers at the National Center for Coffee Research (Cenicafe) said this week.

"According to our historical data this phenomenon causes a significant drop in rainfall in the coffee-growing zone. But when we look at the influence of this drop in rainfall on coffee production we do not note an adverse effect," agroclimatologist Orlando Guzman, of Cenicafe, told Reuters.
"Paradoxically El Nino could be good for coffee because flowering periods are better when dry spells are longer," he added.

Colombia's Institute of Hydrology, Meteorology and Environmental Studies (IDEAM) predicts the El Nino phenomenon will begin to be seen toward the end of this year and will last through the first half of 1998.

Humberto Gomez, head of environmental information at the institute, said the El Nino would likely produce the highest temperatures in December, January and February periods and the driest periods in March, April and May.

He added that while the Andean region and the Atlantic coast would suffer from drought, part of the southwest including Cauca, Valle del Cauca, Narino and Putumayo provinces could see heavier than normal rainfall.

The El Nino is caused by a warming of the Pacific Ocean which interacts with other weather systems and typically produces freak weather conditions such as drought in some areas and heavier than normal rainfall in other areas.
Weather experts meeting this week in Melbourne, Australia, said the latest El Nino could be almost as severe as that of 1982/83 -- the longest and harshest this century.

Cenicafe's Guzman said that rainfall in Colombia's 16 coffee- growing provinces tends to drop by between 10 percent and 15 percent, from the annual average of 32 inches 2,000 millimeters, while the El Nino lasts.
But the severest effects of drought are usually felt in areas below about 4,000 feet 1,200 meters, which are not generally classed as the best coffee producing zones anyway.

During the last El Nino, whose effects were felt throughout 1992, the hardest hit coffee-growing areas were parts of northeast Norte de Santander, central Cundinamarca and southwest Valle del Cauca provinces.
But Guzman added: "It's possible that some production in low- lying areas could be affected by El Nino but the overall national output is unlikely to suffer."
If the dry period strikes in the flowering period of February and March, the main harvest of September/October could be higher than normal, Guzman said.
If the dry spell is most acute in July and August, the development of the main harvest beans could be stunted.

Any potential loss, however, would be likely offset by the beneficial effects that a dry July and August would have on the flowering period of trees producing for the smaller Mitaca harvest, which usually begins the following March/April, and produces about 40 percent of Colombia's total output.

The coffee crop in the 1991/92 coffee year was 17.9 million 60-kg bags and that of the 1992/93 coffee year was 14.9 million bags, some of the highest levels in at least the last 30 years, according to National Coffee Growers' Federation figures.
Production in the 1982/83 coffee year -- during one of the worst El Ninos on record -- production stood at 12.8 million bags.

By comparison, the federation estimates production for the 1996/97 coffee year will be "about 10 million bags" with the figure rising to "about normal" levels of 12 million bags in the 1997/98 coffee year.
(-- Bogota newsroom 571 610 7944.)
